    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Most local AI demos start with a bigger model. I went the other way: a 49.2M parameter model trained from scratch, wrapped in a runtime that does the things a small model is bad at — retrieval, tools and honest missing-source handling.

    A 49M model is not a general assistant. On a no-RAG knowledge probe it scores 2/10. It will not write your backend or answer MMLU. Pretending otherwise is how tiny-model demos lose trust.

    So Atom Zero separates responsibilities:.

    The 21/21 is the product, not the bare model. The benchmark is narrow and authored: tools, memory, retrieval, missing-source behavior and one short generation. It is not MMLU, GSM8K or HumanEval.

    The loop is deliberately boring:.

    A live run produced unapproved_run: 0, then approved_run: done, then a cited answer. The model did not decide what to study and did not mutate its own weights. Weight updates happen only through reviewed feedback -> gated LoRA -> explicit activation/rollback.

    If you run local models on a small GPU, want source-cited notes, or are building a compact RAG/agent reference, I would like to hear what breaks first.

    Industry observers note that apache-2.0 for code and weights. Built on a 6 GB RTX 3050 laptop.

    #92655. Latest Update: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2424 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2424 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model.
    • Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
    • Industry observers note that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

    Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

    Industry observers note that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

    This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

    Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

    Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

    It has been revealed that architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

    Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

    According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

    Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

    In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

    We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

    You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

    Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

    Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

    According to recent reports, SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

    We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

    We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

    In a recent development, MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

    The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

    Over the Still Sea (Qwen 3.8 27B).

    Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • The goal of this project is to build a fully automated, serverless CI/CD (Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment) pipeline on Amazon Web Services (AWS) for a containerized 2048 web game.
    • It has been revealed that packaging the Application with Docker The 2048 game is a static web application made of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files.
    • Sources indicate that serverless Hosting on Amazon ECS Fargate Instead of renting and managing traditional virtual servers (EC2 instances), the application is hosted on Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) using AWS Fargate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The goal of this project is to build a fully automated, serverless CI/CD (Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment) pipeline on Amazon Web Services (AWS) for a containerized 2048 web game. Whenever a developer pushes updated code to the main branch on GitHub, AWS automatically builds a newly introduced Docker container image, stores it securely, and updates the live website without any manual work or server management.

    It has been revealed that packaging the Application with Docker The 2048 game is a static web application made of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files. To make sure it runs reliably in the cloud, it was packaged inside a lightweight Docker container using Nginx (a fast web server) running on Alpine Linux. This keeps the container small and allows it to start up in seconds. The initial container image was uploaded to a private storage registry called Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR).

    Sources indicate that serverless Hosting on Amazon ECS Fargate Instead of renting and managing traditional virtual servers (EC2 instances), the application is hosted on Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) using AWS Fargate. Fargate is a serverless compute engine that runs containers directly. A cluster and service were configured with 0.25 vCPU and 0.5 GB of memory, opening port 80 to the internet so owners can play the game directly through the container's public IP address.

    Sources indicate that connecting GitHub to AWS To detect code changes automatically, the GitHub repository was linked to AWS using AWS Code Connections (via the official AWS GitHub App). This creates a secure webhook connection so that AWS is notified immediately whenever newly introduced commits are pushed to the main branch.

    Automated Building with AWS CodeBuild AWS CodeBuild acts as the automated build engine. Whenever triggered, it releases a temporary build environment, downloads the latest code from GitHub, builds a fresh Docker image, and tags it with both "latest" and the unique 7-character Git commit ID. It then pushes the latest image to Amazon ECR and saves a small tracking file (imagedefinitions.json) into an Amazon S3 bucket so the deployment stage knows exact image details to use.

    Orchestrating the Workflow with AWS CodePipeline AWS CodePipeline ties the entire process together into three automated stages: Source Stage: Pulls the newly pushed code from GitHub.

    Build Stage: Runs AWS CodeBuild to compile the Docker image and push it to Amazon ECR.

    Deploy Stage: Instructs Amazon ECS to patch the live service. ECS performs a zero-downtime rolling update by launching a brand-new container task with the updated image, routing user traffic to it, and safely shutting down the old container task.

    Industry observers note that security and Key Engineering Lessons To keep the pipeline secure, a dedicated IAM service role was created following the principle of least privilege, restricting permissions strictly to the required ECR repository, S3 bucket, ECS service, and GitHub connection. During implementation, three critical configuration requirements were addressed:.

    Industry observers note that enabling Privileged Mode inside CodeBuild so it has permission to run Docker build commands. Granting both modern (codeconnections) and legacy (codestar-connections) permissions in the IAM policy so CodeBuild can authenticate with GitHub during the source download phase. Matching the exact container name between the build output file and the ECS task definition so automated deployments link properly.

    #92651. Reading China's probation rules as a spec: a ladder, an 80% floor, and one ambiguous 'or'

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (997 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Reading China's probation rules as a spec: a ladder, an 80% floor, and one ambiguous 'or'

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, I spent a morning turning one employment-law clause into something a script can check, and the interesting part was not the code.
    • It has been revealed that the subject is probation in a Chinese employment contract.
    • Industry observers note that the boundaries are written in Chinese range notation: "three months and above but under one year", "one year and above but under three years", and so on.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, I spent a morning turning one employment-law clause into something a script can check, and the interesting part was not the code. It was that a single word in the statute — "or" — makes one of the two wage floors unverifiable from the text alone.

    It has been revealed that the subject is probation in a Chinese employment contract. The rules live in four documents: the Labour Contract Law, its 2008 implementing rules, a 2020 Supreme People's Court interpretation, and a 1996 set of rules for foreign employees. The clause I cared about sets how long a probation may run. It is a ladder keyed to the contract term, and the ladder is the part a contract-checker can automate.

    Industry observers note that the boundaries are written in Chinese range notation: "three months and above but under one year", "one year and above but under three years", and so on. The word 以上 includes the boundary and 不满 excludes it. So a contract of exactly twelve months sits in the two-month band, and one of exactly thirty-six months sits in the six-month band. A parser that reads these as plain inequalities gets both boundaries wrong.

    That is the whole reason I wrote a function instead of a checklist: the off-by-one sits exactly where people read fastest.

    According to recent reports, two more rules from the same article are cheap to check and easy to miss. A probation is counted inside the contract term, so a two-year contract with two months of probation still ends at month twenty-four. And a contract that states only a probation term is not a probation at all: the stated period becomes the contract term.

    Article 20 sets the pay floor during probation: not below 80% of the lowest wage for the same post in the unit, or 80% of the wage agreed in the contract, and never below the local minimum wage. The implementing rules repeat the sentence almost verbatim.

    The "or" is doing a lot of work. If the two reference wages differ — say a contract wage of 10,000 and a same-post lowest tier of 9,000 — the text does not say whether the floor is 7,200, 8,000, or the higher of the two. Practice is said to take the higher, which would be 8,000 here, but I found no national document that resolves it. Writing a checker that silently picks one is worse than writing one that refuses and prints both.

    So the function returns both, and the caller decides:.

    The minimum wage is the only unambiguous floor in that dictionary. It is set by province and moves on its own schedule, which is why the function takes it as an input rather than looking it up.

    In a recent development, article 83 is the reason the ladder matters in practice. Where the agreed probation exceeded the cap and was actually served, the employer pays compensation for the months served beyond the cap, measured at the monthly wage that applies after probation ends.

    Two details there are easy to skim past. The measure is the post-probation wage, not the probation wage, so a large step-up at the end inflates the compensation. And the base is the excess months only, not the whole probation.

    The compensation is a separate payment from wages. The months worked are paid anyway; Article 83 adds the excess months again at the post-probation rate. It is not a refund, and it does not void the contract.

    Recent findings suggest that article 21 limits termination during probation to two grounds: Article 39 and the first two items of Article 40. Agreement and resignation are separate routes and are not covered by that limit.

    According to recent reports, the distinction costs money. Termination for "not meeting the recruitment conditions" sits in Article 39 and carries no severance. Termination for incompetence after training sits in Article 40(2), which requires thirty days' notice or one month's wage in lieu, plus severance. An employer who treats probation as a discount on dismissal is reading the wrong article.

    It has been revealed that one procedural asymmetry is worth knowing: where a dismissal is challenged, the employer carries the burden of proof. That is Article 44 of the 2020 interpretation, and it applies to the "not meeting conditions" ground like any other.

    The rule states a probation may be agreed only once between one employer and one worker. I read the article looking for a time limit — a window after which a rehire could carry a upcoming probation — and found none. The restriction is stated without a condition, so a script can treat "has this employer and worker agreed a probation before" as a permanent flag.

    That noted, I could not verify the edge cases: a transfer to an affiliate, a worker who returns a decade later, a probation extended by agreement within the cap. None of those is addressed in the four texts, and I did not read local court practice.

    This is a reading of primary texts, not legal advice. Every article number above was read in the source document rather than taken from a summary, and the arithmetic is mine with assumed wages. The open items — the "or" in Article 20, the extension question, the affiliate question, whether compensation needs a labour-authority order before arbitration — are written out on the site version of this piece, which is the canonical copy:.

    Probation in China: six-month caps and an 80% pay floor.

    If you are checking a contract rather than writing a parser, the ladder plus the excess-month formula covers the part the text settles. The rest needs a lawyer who reads local practice, which is exactly the part I left unfilled.

    Build an AI Label Remover in the Browser: Strip C2PA, IPTC and XMP From Images With JavaScript

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (305 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, instagram, Facebook and Threads add an "AI info" label.
    • Industry observers note that that is why a real photo with one Generative Fill edit gets labelled, and why people search for an AI label remover or an AI image label remover.
    • We keep the ICC colour profile (JPEG APP2, PNG iCCP), otherwise colours shift.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, instagram, Facebook and Threads add an "AI info" label. TikTok says "AI-generated", Pinterest says "AI modified", X says "Made with AI". In most cases these platforms are not analysing pixels. They read metadata inside the file.

    Industry observers note that that is why a real photo with one Generative Fill edit gets labelled, and why people search for an AI label remover or an AI image label remover. In this post we build the core of one in plain JavaScript. It runs fully in the browser, so the image is never uploaded.

    We keep the ICC colour profile (JPEG APP2, PNG iCCP), otherwise colours shift.

    Industry observers note that A JPEG is a sequence of segments: 0xFF, a marker byte, a 2-byte substantial-endian length, then the payload. Image data starts at Start of Scan (0xFFDA), and we copy everything from there unchanged.

    After the 8-byte signature, a PNG is a list of chunks: length (4 bytes), type (4 ASCII bytes), data, CRC.

    Because we never decode the image, the output has the exact same pixels and no quality loss.

    If you just want the finished tool, AI Flag Remover is a free AI label remover built this way, with HEIC/WebP/AVIF support, batch mode and a "keep camera data" option. Disclosure: I build it.

    Only for metadata-based detection. A metadata cleaner does not touch invisible pixel watermarks such as Google's SynthID, and it does not change how pixel-based AI detectors judge an image. It also cannot change a label on a post that is already live.

    It has been revealed that the honest use case is fixing false AI labels on real photos and removing private data such as GPS. If an image is AI-generated, disclose it: platforms and laws like the EU AI Act increasingly require that.

    Taking a high dose of vitamin B6 for a month reduced depression symptoms in people already experiencing them.

    The vitamin helps the brain produce chemical messengers involved in mood regulation.

    The findings suggest a potential role for B6 in treating depression, although larger clinical trials are needed.

    Almost 270 adults, mostly young women, took part in the research.

    They were randomly assigned to take either 100 mg of vitamin B6, vitamin B12 or a placebo each day for around a month.

    Among almost 60 people with at least mild depression symptoms at the start, those taking B6 improved more than those receiving B12 or a placebo.

    Average depression scores fell by about 54 percent in the symptomatic B6 group, compared with 24 percent in the placebo group.

    The benefit remained after accounting for differences in how severe their symptoms had been at the start.

    The findings come from a fresh analysis of data collected in the same research programme that previously reported reduced anxiety after B6 supplementation.

    Vitamin B6 supports several processes involved in regulating mood.

    Dr David Field, the study’s first author, stated:.

    “Vitamin B6 plays a crucial role in the production of several chemical messengers in the brain, including serotonin and GABA, both of which are central to mood regulation.”.

    GABA helps restrain nerve cell activity, contributing to the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain.

    Increasing B6 availability could boost their production, potentially explaining the improvement in depression symptoms.

    Inflammation may also play a role, potentially affecting both depression and how the body uses B6.

    Vitamin B6 occurs naturally in foods including poultry, fish, chickpeas, bananas and fortified cereals.

    However, the trial tested a high supplement dose, rather than a change in everyday food intake.

    High doses of B6 can cause peripheral nerve damage, so the researchers say supplementation at these doses requires medical supervision.

    Larger trials now need to establish the most effective dose, monitor safety and determine whether B6 could help alongside existing depression treatments.

    The study was published in the journal Depression and Anxiety (Field et al., 2026).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

    It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

    Sources indicate that blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

    A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

    A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

    Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

    Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

    To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:.

    Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

    Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many consumers and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

    Recent findings suggest that and that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more swiftly than ever.

    Industry observers note that even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

    Industry observers note that blockchain already being adopted by some significant-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

    Industry observers note that although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

    Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

    Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

    In a recent development, blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

    Sources indicate that have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

    It has been revealed that blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

    Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

    Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

    Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

    I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

    Sources indicate that blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

    It has been revealed that yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

    Industry observers note that coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

    Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

    Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency.

    Sources indicate that generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

    Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain.     #92640. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: Why Learnable Functions on Edges Beat Fixed Activations

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1592 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: Why Learnable Functions on Edges Beat Fixed Activations

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every multilayer perceptron is built on the same deal: the edges carry numbers and the nodes carry the nonlinearity.
    • The Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, proved in 1957, states that any continuous multivariate function on a bounded domain can be written as a finite composition of continuous univariate functions and addition.
    • Industry observers note that that is a striking claim.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every multilayer perceptron is built on the same deal: the edges carry numbers and the nodes carry the nonlinearity. A weight multiplies a signal, a fixed activation such as ReLU or GELU bends it, and the network learns by adjusting the numbers. It works, but the deal is arbitrary. The Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem says there is another way to build a function, one where the edges themselves are learnable functions and the nodes only add. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, or KANs, take that theorem literally, and the result is a model that is more interpretable, more parameter-efficient on structured problems, and surprisingly good at rediscovering symbolic laws from data.

    The Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, proved in 1957, states that any continuous multivariate function on a bounded domain can be written as a finite composition of continuous univariate functions and addition. In its two-layer form:.

    Industry observers note that that is a striking claim. It claims a function of n variables never needs a genuinely multivariate nonlinearity. It only needs univariate functions, applied to single inputs, combined by addition. The outer functions Φq\Phi_qΦq​ and the inner functions ϕq,p\phi_{q,p}ϕq,p​ depend on f, and the theorem says nothing about how smooth they are. In the worst case they can be fractal and pathological, which is why the theorem sat on the shelf for decades as a curiosity rather than a blueprint.

    According to recent reports, the KAN idea is to turn the theorem into a trainable architecture by restricting those univariate functions to a smooth, parameterised family: B-splines. If the true function is reasonably well behaved, a spline can approximate each univariate piece closely, and the network can learn the decomposition from data. The theorem supplies the structure; the splines supply the learnability.

    It has been revealed that an MLP layer is a linear map followed by a fixed nonlinearity applied at each node. A KAN layer inverts that arrangement. Every edge carries a learnable univariate function, and every node simply sums its incoming signals:.

    Sources indicate that there is no activation function at the node at all. The nonlinearity lives entirely on the edges, inside the ϕl,j,i\phi_{l,j,i}ϕl,j,i​ .

    Each edge function is parameterised as a B-spline plus a smooth basis function:.

    Here b(x)=x/(1+e−x)b(x) = x / (1 + e^{-x})b(x)=x/(1+e−x) is the SiLU basis, BiB_iBi​ are B-spline basis functions of order k on a grid of size G, and the coefficients cic_ici​ are the learnable parameters. The grid controls resolution: a coarse grid gives a smooth, low-capacity function, while a fine grid can capture sharp features. One practical advantage is grid extension. A KAN trained on a coarse grid can be refined to a finer grid by fitting the finer spline to the learned function, without retraining from scratch. That is the analogue of increasing resolution in a numerical method, and it gives a principled way to add capacity during training.

    In a recent development, stacking layers composes these univariate functions, so a deep KAN can represent functions whose structure is compositional: a sum of functions of sums of functions, and so on. The width of a layer sets how many univariate pieces are available at that stage, just as width in an MLP sets how many features are available.

    In a recent development, the first payoff is interpretability. In an MLP, the learned object is a weight matrix, and understanding what a single weight means requires tracing it through the rest of the network. In a KAN, the learned object on each edge is a one-dimensional function, and a one-dimensional function can be plotted. You can look at an edge and see that it learned something close to a sine wave, a logarithm, or a saturating curve. After training, edges whose functions are near zero can be pruned, and the remaining functions can be fitted with symbolic expressions, turning the trained network into a readable formula. That is why KANs have attracted attention in scientific machine learning: when the data come from a physical law, the network has a chance of rediscovering the law rather than merely approximating it.

    The second payoff is parameter efficiency on structured problems. A function with a compositional structure, such as f(x,y)=sin⁡(xy)f(x, y) = \sin(x y)f(x,y)=sin(xy) or a polynomial in a few variables, can require a large MLP to approximate to high accuracy, because the MLP must build the structure out of generic piecewise-linear pieces. A KAN can represent the same structure directly, with far fewer parameters. In the original KAN paper, small KANs matched or beat larger MLPs on symbolic regression tasks and on fitting special functions, often by orders of magnitude in parameter count.

    The third payoff is a cleaner inductive bias for low-dimensional problems. Many scientific problems have few inputs and a smooth target with identifiable structure. An MLP treats such a problem as a generic high-dimensional approximation task. A KAN treats it as a composition of univariate pieces, which is a much stronger and often correct prior.

    The cleanest demonstration is symbolic regression. Suppose the data come from a function with multiplicative structure, and you want the model to recover it rather than just interpolate it. Using the pykan library, the workflow is short:.

    Three things about this workflow are worth noting. First, model.plot() is not a debugging aid; it is the main interpretability tool, because each edge function is a plot. Second, pruning is meaningful in a way weight pruning in an MLP is not: removing an edge removes a whole univariate function, and the surviving graph is a readable decomposition of the target. Third, symbolic_formula() closes the loop from data to equation, which is the point of the exercise. If the learned functions are close to sine, exponential, or polynomial pieces, the symbolic fit recovers them, and you can check the recovered formula against held-out data.

    Industry observers note that the same pattern applies to real scientific data. Given measurements of a physical system, a KAN can be trained, pruned, and converted to a candidate formula, which a domain expert can then inspect, test, and refine. That is a different workflow from deploying a black-box predictor, and for science it is often the more valuable one.

    KANs are not a replacement for MLPs, and the honest limitations matter more than the headline results.

    Training is slower. Evaluating a spline on every edge costs more than a matrix multiply followed by a pointwise activation, and the backward pass through the spline coefficients is heavier still. For large models, that cost dominates, and the parameter efficiency on small problems does not translate into a compute advantage at scale.

    Scaling behaviour is unsettled. The original paper reported favourable neural scaling laws for KANs on some tasks, but follow-up work has shown MLPs catching up or overtaking KANs as model and data scale grow, particularly on high-dimensional tasks such as vision and language where the target function has little low-dimensional compositional structure to exploit. No KAN has yet matched a transformer on a large language or vision benchmark, and there is no evidence it should.

    Optimisation is trickier. Spline coefficients interact with each other in ways that weights in an MLP do not, and the loss landscape can be harder to navigate. Grid extension helps, but choosing the grid size, spline order, and regularisation strength adds hyperparameters that an MLP does not have. Too fine a grid overfits; too coarse a grid underfits; and the right choice depends on the smoothness of the unknown target.

    Finally, interpretability has a limit. A KAN is interpretable when the true function is compositional and the learned decomposition is sparse. On a genuinely high-dimensional problem with no such structure, the learned edge functions are arbitrary wiggles, and plotting them tells you nothing. Interpretability is a property of the problem as much as of the model.

    Sources indicate that use a KAN when the problem is low-dimensional, the target is plausibly a composition of simple univariate functions, and you care about the formula as much as the prediction. Scientific modelling, symbolic regression, and small tabular problems with smooth structure are the natural home. Avoid KANs when the inputs are high-dimensional raw signals, when training speed at scale matters, or when a transformer or a large MLP is already known to work well. In those settings, the MLP's simplicity and speed win.

    A practical checklist before training: start with a small width and a coarse grid, and refine the grid only if the fit is underfitting; use the L1-style regularisation on edge magnitudes that the library provides, so pruning has something to work with; plot the edge functions early, not just at the end, because a healthy KAN shows smooth, recognisable curves while a struggling one shows noise; and always validate the symbolic formula on held-out data before believing it, since a spline can fit training noise with a plausible-looking curve.

    In a recent development, MLPs put the learning in the weights and the nonlinearity in fixed activations. KANs put the learning in the functions themselves, with one learnable univariate function per edge and nothing but addition at the nodes. The Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem guarantees that such a decomposition exists; B-splines make it trainable. The result is not a universal replacement for the MLP, but a sharper tool for a specific job: low-dimensional, structured problems where the learned function should be inspected, pruned, and ideally read back as a formula. When the problem fits that description, a KAN can do with a handful of parameters what an MLP needs thousands for, and it can show its working.

    • Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

    An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

    Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers. Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

    Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

    It has been revealed that performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

    Recent findings suggest that smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a massive opportunity.

    The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

    An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

    It has been revealed that publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

    In a recent development, A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program. Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

    Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

    Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:.

    One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

    Recent findings suggest that commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

    Who manages your affiliate program?

    Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

    • I wanted a plain answer to a plain question: what does it cost to keep one Postgres database running all month on a managed service?
    • So we priced the same setup on 11 providers at two sizes:.
    • According to recent reports, the rules: one database, always on (730 hours), single node with no standby, in London where offered (Railway in Amsterdam, Render in Frankfurt, Heroku in its EU region).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I wanted a plain answer to a plain question: what does it cost to keep one Postgres database running all month on a managed service? Not the "from" price, but the bill once storage and any initiative fee you must pay first are added.

    So we priced the same setup on 11 providers at two sizes:.

    According to recent reports, the rules: one database, always on (730 hours), single node with no standby, in London where offered (Railway in Amsterdam, Render in Frankfurt, Heroku in its EU region). Storage and any compulsory strategy fee are included. Prices are in US dollars, before VAT, and were checked in November 2026. They change, so check the vendor's page before you commit.

    In a recent development, heroku is cheapest on paper, but it doesn't publish Essential-1's memory, so it may not match 1 GB. The cheapest with a stated 1 GB are DigitalOcean at $15.15 and AWS RDS at $15.80.

    Neon's figure keeps the compute on all month. A Neon database that scales to zero when idle costs less: Neon's own "typical" Launch figure is $15 a month.

    Recent findings suggest that railway's figure is an estimate. It bills the RAM and CPU a service actually uses, and we assumed the database holds all 16 GB and averages 10% of its CPU; each extra 10% adds $8. Heroku's Standard-3 ($400) has only 2 vCPU and 15.25 GB, so Standard-4 is its first plan that fits.

    Almost everyone bills storage separately, per GB a month: Neon $0.35, Render $0.30, Google Cloud SQL $0.204 in London, Railway $0.15, AWS RDS $0.133, and Supabase $0.125 after the 8 GB it includes.

    At 200 GB that's a real line on the bill: $70.00 at Neon, $60 at Render, $40.80 at Google Cloud SQL, $30 at Railway and $26.60 at AWS RDS.

    Minimums matter at the small end. AWS's gp3 storage starts at 20 GiB, so a 10 GB database pays for 20. Azure's Burstable servers can't go below a 32 GiB disk. Aiven's cheaper plans are fixed at 8 GB of storage, so its cheapest proposal that holds 10 GB is Startup-4 at $75, the same plan and price as a 2 vCPU / 4 GB database.

    Neon, AWS, Google Cloud, DigitalOcean, Aiven and Heroku charge no platform fee.

    Sources indicate that on 15 October 2026 DigitalOcean changed its database prepares. Accounts that have never created a database, and every account from 30 November, can only create Standard Edition clusters up to 4 GiB, with no standby nodes.

    It has been revealed that so a 16 GB database, or any high availability, now means Advanced Edition, from $135.75 a month. The 16 GB setup above is $283 there. The 16 GiB Standard intends still shown on the pricing page ($198.55 and $244.35) can't be bought by fresh customers. If you priced DigitalOcean before mid-October, price it again.

    Sources indicate that at 1 GB, platform fees and storage minimums move the order as much as the compute price does. At 16 GB the range runs from $198 to $750, and the shape of the plan (burstable or not, more RAM than you asked for, which edition a new account may buy) matters more than the hourly rate.

    Sources indicate that I keep the full table, with every price linked to the vendor's own page, including a third size (2 vCPU, 4 GB, 50 GB) and the standby prices. Prices were checked on 9 November 2026.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that if you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

    Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

    In a recent development, seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers.

    In a recent development, phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

    According to recent reports, hubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

    When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

    According to recent reports, acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include massive brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and firm-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

    MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool reveals you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

    Recent findings suggest that copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

    According to recent reports, yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

    Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

    Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

    It has been revealed that there are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, latest marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Password Pusher creates expiring links for passwords, text, files and URLs. ZoomEye returned zero matches for app="Password Pusher" and 537 for title="Password Pusher" on 2026-11-22, using sub_type=all, page 1 and page size 1.

    The zero application result is a discovery limitation. The title result is the usable lead, although it can include documentation and hosted-service pages.

    The matches are not confirmed deployments or exposed pushes.

    The recipient uses a push link. The link may expire, allow a limited number of views, or require a passphrase. That path is intentionally available to someone outside the organization.

    According to recent reports, the administrator path is different. The official administration documentation describes /admin, a system-admin role and options such as two-factor authentication. The API v2 documentation describes bearer-token authentication for creating, retrieving and managing pushes.

    Industry observers note that an exposed application does not mean an exposed admin account. Review the routes separately. A public push should not provide management rights, and an API token should not be pasted into a push.

    Industry observers note that look for owned Password Pusher deployments by title, certificate and service owner. Record the public base URL, version, authentication mode and whether the admin dashboard is reachable.

    It has been revealed that inspect the reverse proxy rules that expose /admin, the API and public push routes. If the service is meant for a small team, restrict administration to SSO or a management network.

    Industry observers note that review API token scope and lifetime. Remove tokens that belong to former staff or abandoned integrations. Check whether a token can manage other users or only create a push.

    Industry observers note that set expiration and view limits that reflect the sensitivity of the content. A short-lived link is easier to contain than one that remains valid until someone remembers to revoke it.

    Industry observers note that passphrases help when the link travels through a channel that may retain it. Send the link and the passphrase through different channels where possible.

    Recent findings suggest that do not put secret values in application logs, analytics, browser page titles or notification previews. Review inbound email and chat scanners that may open links automatically. A scanner can consume a one-time link before the recipient does.

    Alert on new administrator accounts, token creation, changes to authentication settings, repeated failed passphrase attempts and a sudden rise in push creation.

    Correlate an admin login with reverse-proxy and application logs. Keep enough metadata to identify the source and route without recording the secret.

    In a recent development, the 537 title matches provide a broad candidate set. The absence of an app fingerprint means the title and page structure need manual review.

    Sources indicate that state that limitation in any report. The useful question is not how many pages mention Password Pusher. It is which owned services separate public push access from administrative and API authority.

    5 Types Of Brain-Affecting Drugs Still Prescribed Despite Safety Warnings

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.
    • Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.
    • One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

    Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

    One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.

    These drugs can increase the risk of confusion, falls and hospitalisation, particularly in people whose thinking and memory are already impaired.

    Despite decades of warnings, people with cognitive impairment were more likely to receive these prescriptions than those with normal cognition.

    The research examined five categories of medication flagged by prescribing guidelines for older adults:.

    Only antidepressants with strong anticholinergic properties were included in this category.

    Anticholinergic medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, learning and concentration.

    Blocking its action can cause confusion and other unwanted effects, especially in older adults.

    Benzodiazepines, which may be prescribed for anxiety or sleep problems, can cause excessive drowsiness and increase the risk of falls.

    Some medicines also take longer to leave the body as people age, allowing their effects to persist or accumulate.

    The researchers analysed survey information linked to medical insurance records from almost 4,900 Americans aged 65 and over.

    They examined prescribing over nine years, counting prescriptions for at least four weeks’ supply.

    Around 17 percent of people with normal cognition received at least one potentially inappropriate prescription, compared with almost 22 percent of those with cognitive impairment without dementia.

    Among people with dementia, the proportion reached 25 percent.

    Across the older adults studied, prescribing fell from around 20 percent at the beginning of the study period to 16 percent at the end.

    Much of the decline reflected fewer prescriptions for benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping medicines.

    However, prescribing rates for the other three drug groups did not change significantly.

    By the final year, more than two-thirds of people receiving these potentially inappropriate prescriptions lacked a documented clinical reason for at least one of them.

    A potentially inappropriate medicine can still be justified when its expected benefits outweigh its risks.

    The practical question is whether each prescription remains suitable for the person taking it.

    Dr Annie Yang, the study’s first author, emphasised the importance of patients and carers reviewing these medicines with their physicians:.

    “While CNS-active prescriptions may be appropriate in some cases, it is key for older patients or their caregivers to work closely with their physicians to ensure that these medications are appropriate to their cases.

    When inappropriate, patients and their care teams should consider alternative treatments and consider whether it might be safe to taper or stop the medication.”.

    The study was published in JAMA (Yang et al., 2026).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    Breaking: What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S.
    • Recent findings suggest that “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” noted Jadon Urogdy.
    • Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

    Recent findings suggest that “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” noted Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”.

    Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

    Urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

    Fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

    Working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

    Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

    Industry observers note that “There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” stated Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”.

    Natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

    For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”.

    “We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin said.

    What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

    While Gen Z respondents who said they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

    “We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” remarked Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

    Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

    Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

    Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

    The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

    For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy stated tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

    Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related complications than average.

    It has been revealed that another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people said the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

    “I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy remarked. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”.

    Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

    It has been revealed that “We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” remarked Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

    Recent findings suggest that fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio mentioned. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”.

She attained an M.A. in Media, Culture, & Communication from NYU and a B.Sc. in Sociology from LSE. She was previously the digital communications manager for the Division of Social Sciences at UC Santa Cruz.
