    #92624. The Overlooked Ways Love Shows Up in Urban Spaces

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1120 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

    The Overlooked Ways Love Shows Up in Urban Spaces

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings.
    • But, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—Newly introduced York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue.
    • In a recent development, my former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings. Why? Because social science research on life in America’s cities is desperately incomplete. Much like the vision of urban life that permeates most of American popular culture, social science research imagines urban areas as sites of overwhelmedness, disengagement, social and moral crisis, threat, and violence.

    But, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—Newly introduced York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue. People in urban contexts, including those living in high-stress, oversurveilled, underresourced communities, draw daily from deep wells of love, compassion, empathy, kindness, and generosity in the service of caring for each other. From holding doors open for one another, to offering seats on buses and trains, to stopping to help with directions, to paying unexpected compliments, city-dwellers create environments that are saturated with powerful but easily missed acts of care.

    In a recent development, my former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces. Through surveys and interviews, we have sought to understand how adults residing in significant cities define love, how they see love being expressed, and their views of the cascading effects of giving and receiving care, generosity, and love.

    Industry observers note that we have learned that the decision to express love and care for others in large cities is not simply a moral or emotional decision. We offer two examples of the lens needed to notice the presence of love in cities.

    First, we have learned that identities matter in experiences of compassion, love, and care between strangers. Urban dwellers’ identity (for example, race or gender), lived experience, context, familial, cultural, and legal systems’ realities work together to shape decisions about whether to extend acts of love to people you do not know. For example, Kehinde, a 26-year-old African American man living in a large, densely populated city, described his experience of giving and receiving kindness, care, and love in his city as shaped by how he navigates other people seeing him as a Black man.

    “I will see folks all the time that may need a hand with their bags or crossing the street or just little things like that. And I take a second, hesitate,” Kehinde says. “I don’t want to scare them. I don’t want to come off as a threat.”.

    According to recent reports, to get through these moments, Kehinde describes engaging in a practice of analysis and shape-shifting. Before he steps in to offer help, he assesses the environment and changes the way he carries himself so that people will perceive him as a possible helper rather than as a threat. He claims: “I smile a lot more. My voice might change a bit.” He might shrink his body and keep his head down, to avoid seeming intimidating. After helping someone, he moves along without lingering. Reflecting, he acknowledges not being his full, true self in these interactions. “I have to realize I’ve been socialized—made to believe that this is what I need to do in order to navigate the situation.” Kehinde’s story highlights the point that identities matter in economies of care. The images and stereotypes that we construct about people come at a cost even in moments of compassion. Stereotypes affect who we perceive as deserving of care, concern, and protection. Stereotypes also inform our expectations about who can be trusted to help. Stereotyping is not unique to urban settings. But because urban settings tend to be especially diverse spaces, they create abundant opportunities to study how identities and the social scripts we hold affect the way that strangers care for each other across lines of difference. What Kehinde and others bring to the fore is the reality that the targets of stereotyping are aware of the ways that they are perceived. They learn that to be seen as helpful rather than as threatening, they need to read situations correctly, make adjustments to their approaches (e.g., keep “appropriate” distance), and exit situations strategically. Targets of stereotyping must strike a balance between their own deep-seated motivations to behave caringly and their desire to stay safe. For individuals like Kehinde, miscalculations can be costly. If, in the effort to behave lovingly and compassionately, someone is misidentified as a threat, that can lead to a range of consequences from being rebuffed and embarrassed to becoming the target of violence, arrest, or death. The end result is that people consciously or unconsciously learn the rules of engagement around helping strangers.

    This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

    It has been revealed that A second lesson that has emerged from studying love in urban settings is that love lives in the built environment of cities. I highlight this lesson in my Positive Psychology in Urban Settings classes. Cities are often saturated with murals, billboards, and symbols that convey messages of love, solidarity, and belonging. As residents move through neighborhood streets, they may encounter signs prominently posted in shop windows or near the entrances of religious institutions that remind them that “Black Lives Matter,” “Love Is Love,” or “Immigrants Are Welcome Here.” People display rainbow flags and national flags from apartment windows, on cars, and in other spaces, declaring both their own identities and pride for and solidarity with those identities. The architecture of urban spaces may also play a role in expressions of love and care. In many urban neighborhoods, porches, stoops, and front steps serve as places of connection and care. Simple greetings (e.g., “Morning, baby!,” “You doing good?”) voiced by neighbors sitting on their steps serve as ways of spatializing love, care, and connection in urban landscapes.

    I return here to my initial point. Our studies of urban areas are desperately incomplete and will remain incomplete until we more fully examine how various forms of human goodness—including love and care—flourish in urban settings. Likewise, our understandings of love and care will remain underdeveloped until we explore how these experiences emerge in the most densely populated, diverse, complex social structures in which people live. We will truly understand love when we understand how it is titrated through place, context, history, culture, religion, structures of power, identities, and a host of individual and relational factors. Urban centers give us powerful opportunities to know love.

    Jacqueline Mattis, Ph.D., is dean of the School of Arts and Sciences at Rutgers University-Newark. She studies human goodness in urban contexts.

    This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

    A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

    Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

    Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, mentioned:.

    “A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”.

    The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

    One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

    The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

    Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

    After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

    These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

    The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

    Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

    The memory findings were more complicated.

    Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

    By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

    One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

    Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in upcoming information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

    However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

    Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

    Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

    Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

    These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

    The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

    Blood samples also showed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

    Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

    The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

    In a recent development, psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004.     What Happier People Tend To Believe About Others

    📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

    Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

    The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially notable at these ages.

    Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

    The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

    The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

    Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

    The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

    Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

    For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

    In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

    The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

    The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

    General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

    All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people showed the strongest connection.

    Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

    Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

    These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

    Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

    This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

    Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

    The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

    One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

    Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

    Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

    The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

    A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

    Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

    Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, stated:.

    “But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”.

    The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

    “When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”.

    The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    #92614. Breaking: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1550 w)

    Breaking: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, finding love is big business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business.
    • The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages.
    • As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this newly introduced generation of dating apps.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, finding love is big business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

    The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app customers to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

    As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this newly introduced generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

    So if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

    Industry observers note that what about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

    Recent findings suggest that perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user states they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

    In a recent development, if the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

    According to recent reports, what do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

    Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

    The truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

    This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

    With the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

    Recent findings suggest that I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

    An alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

    Amie M. Gordon, Ph.D., is a social-personality psychologist who takes a dynamic, dyadic approach to investigating the affective, social-cognitive, and biological processes that shape interpersonal relationships. Her research has been published in top academic journals as well as featured in popular news outlets such as The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Atlantic. She received her PhD in Social-Personality Psychology from UC Berkeley and her BA in Psychology from UCLA. She blogs for Psychology Today in Between You and Me, and is currently completing a postdoctoral research fellowship at the University of California, San Francisco.
